title: Measure for Measure
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — An apartment in the Duke's palace
openingText: Vincentio, Duke of Vienna, has decided to leave his city in the hands of a deputy. The laws against fornication have grown lax under his rule, and he means to absent himself while a strict man enforces them.
about:
The Duke of Vienna pretends to leave the city and hands authority over to his rigorous deputy, Angelo. Angelo immediately enforces a long-neglected law against fornication and sentences young Claudio to death for getting his fiancée pregnant. Claudio's sister Isabella — a novice on the point of taking vows in a strict convent — comes to plead for his life. Angelo discovers, to his horror, that he is sexually obsessed with her and offers her a bargain: Claudio's life in exchange for her virginity.

The Duke, watching all of this in disguise as a friar, intervenes. He arranges a 'bed-trick' in which Angelo's spurned fiancée, Mariana, takes Isabella's place in the dark. Angelo, believing he has slept with Isabella, sends an order for Claudio's execution anyway. The Duke saves Claudio by substituting the head of a dead prisoner. He then stages a public unmasking in the city square, in which he is restored to power, Angelo is sentenced and pardoned, Mariana is married to Angelo, Claudio is restored to Juliet — and the Duke proposes marriage to Isabella, who, in a silence Shakespeare leaves for the actor to fill, never answers.

Shakespeare wrote Measure for Measure around 1604, in the same stretch as All's Well That Ends Well. It has been classified as a comedy, a 'problem play,' and a dark comedy, and the question of whether it earns its happy ending has been argued for four centuries. It contains some of Shakespeare's most extraordinary verse — Isabella's pleas in Act 2, Claudio's 'Ay, but to die, and go we know not where' — and one of his strangest endings.

angleCards.title: Isabella's choice.
angleCards.text: Isabella is the only novice nun in Shakespeare. Angelo asks her for her virginity in exchange for her brother's life. She refuses. She tells Claudio his death is the lesser horror. The play takes seriously what almost no other Shakespeare play takes seriously: a woman saying no.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Measure for Measure as the play of Isabella's refusal: what her vow costs her, what she owes her brother, and how Shakespeare honours the answer she gives.

angleCards.title: Angelo.
angleCards.text: Angelo begins the play as the model of austere virtue and discovers, the first time temptation looks at him, that he has none. He is one of Shakespeare's most chilling portraits — a man who knows what he is doing while he does it and cannot stop.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Angelo's collapse — the public severity, the private bargain with Isabella, the order to kill Claudio anyway — as Shakespeare's study of how a man learns what he is.

angleCards.title: The Duke in disguise.
angleCards.text: The Duke spends most of the play wandering Vienna disguised as a friar, listening to confessions, arranging bed-tricks, and engineering the resolution. He is the play's puppet-master, and the question of his moral standing is one of the things audiences argue about most.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Duke's experiment — leaving Angelo to enforce the laws, watching the city from disguise, engineering the final unmasking — and decide what Shakespeare thinks of a ruler who tests his deputy with other people's lives.

angleCards.title: The silence at the end.
angleCards.text: The Duke proposes marriage to Isabella in the last minute of the play. She does not answer. Shakespeare wrote no line for her. The pause is the most famous silence in the canon.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to attend to the closing silence — the Duke's two proposals and Isabella's lack of reply — as the play's deliberate refusal to give us the ending it appears to promise.

cast.name: Vincentio, Duke of Vienna
cast.description: The ruler of Vienna, who hands his city over to Angelo while pretending to travel abroad. He spends most of the play disguised as a friar, manipulating events, listening to confessions, and finally re-emerging in his own person at the city gate. His motives remain a question.

cast.name: Angelo
cast.description: Vincentio's hand-picked deputy, a man known throughout Vienna for severe virtue. He enforces the old law against fornication and sentences Claudio to death — then propositions Claudio's sister, then orders Claudio killed anyway. One of the most disturbing studies of moral collapse in Shakespeare.

cast.name: Isabella
cast.description: Claudio's sister, a novice about to take her vows in a strict convent. She comes out of the cloister to plead for her brother's life, refuses Angelo's bargain, and is the play's moral conscience. Her last act on stage is a silence.

cast.name: Claudio
cast.description: A young Viennese gentleman engaged to Juliet, with whom he has anticipated the marriage ceremony. Sentenced by Angelo to death under the resurrected fornication law. His prison scenes with the Duke and Isabella are the play's central dialogue on death and survival.

cast.name: Mariana
cast.description: A woman to whom Angelo was once betrothed and whom he abandoned when her dowry was lost at sea. She still loves him. The Duke uses her in the bed-trick to substitute for Isabella, and at the end of the play she pleads for the life of the man who jilted her.

cast.name: Lucio
cast.description: A loud, scurrilous gentleman of Vienna, friend to Claudio, customer of the brothels, and the play's comic engine. He spends the central acts unwittingly slandering the disguised Duke to his face, and is punished for it in the closing scene by being made to marry the prostitute he has dishonoured.

acclaim.quote: There is in this play, throughout, an effort to express something deeply felt, even when the means are not what may be called dramatic.
Of all his plays, Measure for Measure is the one most exclusively addressed to the conscience.
acclaim.context: Appreciations, with an Essay on Style, 1889

whyItMatters.title: Isabella's Refusal
whyItMatters.body: Almost no woman in Shakespeare gets to refuse a man in power as completely as Isabella does. Angelo, the deputy of Vienna, has her brother under sentence of death. Angelo tells her she can save Claudio by yielding her virginity to him. He uses the language of judicial procedure to wrap the threat. Isabella, who has been at the convent door, sees through it at once and refuses. Then she does something even harder. She goes to her brother in his cell and tells him, after he has begged her to save his life, that she cannot. 'More than our brother is our chastity,' she tells him. Claudio's reply — 'Ay, but to die, and go we know not where; / To lie in cold obstruction and to rot' — is one of the most famous death-speeches in the canon. Isabella refuses him too. She tells him she will pray for his death but will not buy his life. Whatever modern audiences make of her vow, the moral force of her refusal is what the play is built on, and what makes the Duke's intervention afterwards feel either like grace or like a violation, depending on how you read it.

whyItMatters.title: The Problem Play
whyItMatters.body: Measure for Measure is the play that gave critics the category 'problem play.' It is officially a comedy. It has a substitute bed-trick, a public unmasking, four weddings at the end, and no on-stage death. It also has a deputy demanding sex in exchange for a man's life, a novice telling her brother to die, and a final silence from the heroine that swallows the marriage offer made to her. The play does not settle. Each generation of critics has argued about whether the ending works, whether the Duke is benevolent or sinister, whether Isabella's silence is consent or refusal, and whether marrying Angelo to Mariana is justice. The Romantics found it offensive; Coleridge called it 'a hateful work.' The twentieth century rehabilitated it as one of Shakespeare's deepest works on the limits of law and the cost of mercy. The play is what it is precisely because it refuses to resolve. The 'problem' is not a defect; it is the form.

whyItMatters.title: The Silence
whyItMatters.body: In the final minute of the play, after Angelo has been pardoned, Claudio restored, Lucio married to a whore, and order ostensibly reset, the Duke turns to Isabella and proposes. He proposes twice. Shakespeare writes no line for her in reply, in either instance. The play ends with the Duke walking offstage and Isabella following him, or not, depending on the production. Some directors stage her accepting. Some stage her refusing. Some stage her standing absolutely still while the Duke walks off alone. Most modern productions stage some version of the third. The silence is the most famous in Shakespeare, and the play's defining demand on its audience: to make sense of an ending the text deliberately refuses to provide. Whatever Shakespeare meant — and the question of what he meant has been argued for four centuries — Isabella's silence is the place where the comedy stops, the play stops, and the audience is handed the unfinished question to take home.
